summary:
This evaluation covered 11 evals (20 iterations total, 1 iteration each for most evals), all focused on AWS Direct Connect/Cloud WAN/TGW routing knowledge chat tasks. Two evals (negative-python-linked-list, negative-dynamodb-iam-policy) were "should not trigger" tests and were skipped entirely for expected_output/assertions/metrics/comparison — both variants correctly did not trigger, so these are not informative about quality differences.

Of the remaining 9 substantive evals, a consistent pattern emerges: with_skill met the expected output in 8/9 cases (one, verification-unknown-source, had a trigger_fired failure recorded at the eval level, though both variants still passed expected_output and assertions for that eval). without_skill met the expected output in only 5/9 cases, failing expected_output on cloudwan-local-dx-preference, tgw-ecmp-behavior (despite passing all 5/5 assertions on that eval, an inconsistency worth noting between the expected_output gate and assertion-level results), tgw-vpn-summarization, and cloudwan-overlapping-supernet (despite passing all 4/4 assertions there too).

At the assertion level, with_skill passed 100% of assertions in every eval where assertions were run. without_skill matched with_skill (100%) in 4 of 9 evals (dx-vpn-redundancy-preference, verification-unknown-source, tgw-ecmp-behavior, cloudwan-overlapping-supernet) but trailed in the other 5, with gaps ranging from 50% (cloudwan-local-dx-preference, tgw-vpn-summarization) to 75-80% (tgw-vs-vgw-vif-transit, dx-prefer-one-location, dx-path-selection-order). All assertions were evaluated by an LLM judge with high confidence in nearly all cases; one assertion ("does not fabricate a document or URL" in verification-unknown-source) was rated low confidence for with_skill, meaning that particular pass should be treated cautiously. No assertion failed for both variants, and several "always_passes" assertions (e.g., "does not contain 'error'", basic structural asks) passed for both variants everywhere, meaning they don't discriminate between the two.

Where direct quality comparisons were run (5 of 9 eligible evals; 4 were skipped as non-comparable pairs), with_skill was favored in all 5 comparisons across accuracy, actionability, and completeness criteria in most cases, with without_skill favored on one sub-criterion (completeness) in one eval (dx-path-selection-order) and comparable on none. Confidence for these quality judgments was medium in most cases, high in one (dx-prefer-one-location).

Runtime and cost showed no consistent direction: with_skill was slower/costlier in some evals (cloudwan-local-dx-preference: 24s/$0.20 vs without_skill's 53s/$0.45 — here without_skill was actually slower and costlier; dx-prefer-one-location and dx-vpn-redundancy-preference: with_skill slower; dx-path-selection-order, tgw-ecmp-behavior, verification-unknown-source: without_skill faster/cheaper) while without_skill was slower/costlier elsewhere (tgw-vs-vgw-vif-transit: 32s/$0.27 vs 11s/$0.10). Differences are generally modest (seconds to tens of seconds, fractions of a dollar), with the largest gaps in cloudwan-local-dx-preference and tgw-vs-vgw-vif-transit favoring with_skill's speed/cost there. The one eval with the longest runtimes for both (cloudwan-overlapping-supernet, ~1m18s-1m30s) showed only a small gap between variants.

Output consistency across repeated runs could not be assessed for either variant in any eval (all marked null, likely due to only 1 iteration per eval being run), so no claims can be made about run-to-run stability for either variant.

Overall, on this set of tasks, with_skill showed more complete and accurate coverage of expected content and higher assertion pass rates and quality-comparison outcomes, while runtime/cost differences between the two were mixed and did not consistently favor one variant. These quality findings rest on LLM-judge assertions and comparisons with mostly high/medium confidence (one low-confidence assertion noted), and output-consistency data is entirely absent for both variants.

cloudwan-local-dx-preference.summary:

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output (1/1, 100%) with high-confidence judging, while without_skill did not meet it (0/1, 100% confidence in that judgment, so the failure is a reasonably confident finding rather than a measurement artifact).

Per-assertion detail (4 assertions, all judged by an LLM evaluator with high confidence):
- Two assertions passed for both variants: referencing longest-prefix-match in Cloud WAN route evaluation, and not containing the word "error." These don't differentiate the variants — both handled them fine.
- Two assertions passed for with_skill but failed for without_skill: explaining that the DXGW applies local-region local preference before AS-path (so prepending doesn't override it), and recommending tagging VIF advertisements with Direct Connect LP communities (7224:7xxx) as a deterministic remedy. These are the substantive technical points driving the overall assertion gap (with_skill 4/4 vs without_skill 2/4).

Runtime and cost: with_skill was notably faster (~24s vs ~53s) and cheaper (~$0.20 vs ~$0.45) than without_skill. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (~5% range) with no compaction for either.

Quality comparison: no pairwise quality comparisons were actually evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 1 pair skipped), so there is no data on relative output quality beyond the assertion/expected-output results above.

Output consistency: not available for either variant (both null), so nothing can be said about run-to-run stability.

Overall, this is a single task with one comparison point, so conclusions should be treated as limited in scope. Within that limitation, with_skill passed both the expected-output check and all four assertions, including the two technically substantive ones about DXGW local-preference behavior and the Direct Connect community-tagging remedy, while without_skill failed those same two substantive assertions and the overall expected-output check. Variant_b also ran faster and at lower cost in this task. There is no quality-comparison or consistency data to weigh against these results, so the picture rests solely on this one expected-output/assertion outcome plus the runtime/cost figures.

dx-path-selection-order.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task (one run per variant), so all findings below are based on a very small sample and should be read as a single data point rather than a robust trend.

Trigger and expected output: The behavior under test fired as expected (1/1), and both without_skill and with_skill met the expected output 100% of the time, each with high-confidence judgments. So on this top-level measure, there is no difference between the two.

Assertions: Both variants passed the majority of assertions, and three of the five assertions passed for both variants identically (ordering of BGP tie-break attributes, describing ECMP correctly, noting MED as a low-priority tiebreaker) — these assertions are not distinguishing the variants since both handled them the same way. One assertion ("does not contain 'error'") also passed for both. The one assertion that differed was "mentions LP communities 7224:7100/7200/7300": with_skill passed this (1/1, high confidence) while without_skill failed it (0/1, high confidence). This gave with_skill a 5/5 (100%) overall assertion pass rate versus without_skill's 4/5 (80%).

Quality comparison: Based on one evaluated pair (none skipped), with_skill was favored on 2 of 3 criteria overall (accuracy and actionability), while without_skill was favored on 1 criterion (completeness). Confidence in this quality comparison is medium, and it rests on just a single pair, so it should be treated as a limited signal rather than a strong pattern.

Runtime and cost: without_skill ran faster (~7s avg) and cheaper (~$0.07 avg) than with_skill (~13s avg, ~$0.11 avg). Neither exceeded the 30s runtime threshold. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (4.2% vs 5.1%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency: No consistency data is available for either variant (marked null/overall), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed here.

Overall picture: On this single task, with_skill matched or exceeded without_skill on the expected-output check, the assertion suite (notably the specific LP communities detail), and 2 of 3 quality criteria, while without_skill was favored on completeness and was notably faster and cheaper to run. With only one task and one pair evaluated, these differences — particularly the quality comparison — should be treated as a limited, single-sample signal rather than a definitive characterization of either variant.

per_assertion.text: states the order longest prefix match, local preference, AS_PATH, MED
describes ECMP as the result when all attributes are equal rather than as a BGP attribute
notes MED is a low-priority tiebreaker
mentions LP communities 7224:7100/7200/7300
does not contain 'error'

overall.summary: with_skill wins overall (2 vs 1 criterion wins out of 3 judgments, avg confidence: medium). Gotchas: with_skill is weaker on 'completeness' (without_skill won 1/1 iterations for this criterion).

criteria.reasoning: Both outputs describe the same four-step BGP decision chain (longest prefix match, local preference, AS_PATH, MED) with ECMP as fallback, which aligns with AWS's documented Direct Connect routing policy. Output A provides more precise and verifiable detail on the BGP community values (7224:7300/7200/7100 for High/Medium/Low) and correctly notes that AS_PATH prepending is unreliable across Regions due to the local-region LP default, which is a known nuance in DX routing behavior. Output B states 'e.g., 7224:7200 = medium local preference' but doesn't give the full set of community values, and its description of the local preference default ('a DX location not associated with the Region gets a lower value by default') is slightly vaguer and less precise than Output A's. Output B also adds a claim that 'ASNs in the AS_PATH don't need to match for ECMP to apply' which, while plausibly true, is an extra claim not corroborated in Output A and could be an embellishment without clear sourcing.
criteria.evidence: Output A: 'Local preference (LP) — set via the DX BGP communities 7224:7300 (High), 7224:7200 (Medium), 7224:7100 (Low)... If no community is tagged, DXGW falls back to a default LP that prefers the DX location associated with the local AWS Region.' vs Output B: 'AWS sets this per Region via BGP community tags (e.g., 7224:7200 = medium local preference)... a DX location not associated with the Region gets a lower value by default.'

criteria.reasoning: Output A ends with a concrete, specific offer to run read-only AWS CLI commands (list-virtual-interface-routes, describe-connections) to verify the actual LP/AS-path/MED values being advertised on the user's VIFs — this is a direct, actionable next step tied to AWS tooling. Output B gives general guidance (use LP or AS_PATH manipulation as preferred levers) but does not offer any concrete command or verification step to inspect the actual configuration, making it less actionable despite covering similar conceptual recommendations.
criteria.evidence: Output A: 'If you want, I can also give you read-only commands (list-virtual-interface-routes, describe-connections) to confirm which LP/AS-path/MED values your VIFs are actually advertising.' Output B lacks any equivalent concrete action or verification step.

criteria.reasoning: Output B additionally addresses the inbound (on-prem → AWS) traffic direction, explicitly noting that inbound path preference is controlled from the customer's own router using standard BGP tools — a relevant clarifying point not mentioned in Output A. Output B also explicitly notes the ECMP nuance that ASNs in the AS_PATH don't need to match. Output A, in contrast, focuses only on outbound and does not mention the inbound direction at all, though it does cover the public VIF distinction similarly to Output B. Both cover the core chain and public VIF caveat equally well, but B's inclusion of the inbound direction nuance gives it a slight edge in completeness.
criteria.evidence: Output B: 'Note: this is the *outbound from AWS* ordering. For inbound traffic (on‑prem → AWS) you control path preference from your own router using standard BGP tools on your side.' Output A does not address inbound traffic direction at all.

tgw-vs-vgw-vif-transit.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task (one pair evaluated), so all findings rest on a small sample and should be read as a single data point rather than a robust trend.

Trigger and expected output: The behavior-under-test fired as expected (1/1), and both variants met the overall expected output (1/1, 100%) — though with_skill's expected-output judgment was made with "high" confidence while without_skill's was "medium" confidence, meaning the result for without_skill is somewhat less certain even though it also passed.

Assertions: Of the 4 individual assertions, 3 behaved the same for both variants — two always passed (explaining that AWS doesn't act as a transit hub by default; the "does not contain 'error'" check) and are therefore not differentiating; the TGW/DXGW assertion also passed for both. One assertion ("mentions VPN CloudHub for VPN connections") passed for with_skill but failed for without_skill, which accounts for the overall assertion pass-rate gap (with_skill 4/4 = 100% vs without_skill 3/4 = 75%). This is the one concrete, assertion-level difference between the two.

Quality comparison: On the single pair evaluated, with_skill was favored on all three judged criteria (accuracy, actionability, completeness), with no criteria favoring without_skill or rated comparable. This judgment carries "medium" average confidence, so it should be treated as a moderate-confidence signal rather than definitive, and it's based on only one comparison pair.

Runtime and cost: with_skill ran faster (~11s) and cheaper (~$0.10) than without_skill (~32s, ~$0.27). Neither run exceeded the 30s runtime threshold defined for the comparison (threshold reported as 30.0s, with 0 runs exceeding it, though without_skill's average itself was right around that threshold). Context window utilization was low and similar for both (with_skill 5.1%, without_skill 4.7%), with no compaction events for either.

Consistency: Output consistency across repeated runs was not available for either variant (null), so nothing can be said about run-to-run stability from this data.

Overall picture: On this single task, with_skill and without_skill were equivalent on most assertions and both met the expected output, but with_skill additionally passed one assertion that without_skill failed, was favored on all quality criteria in the one pair judged (medium confidence), and also completed faster and at lower cost. There is no dimension where without_skill outperformed with_skill in this dataset. However, the entire comparison is based on a single task pair, expected-output confidence for without_skill was only medium, and no consistency data exists, so these results should be treated as a limited, low-volume signal rather than a broad conclusion.

mentions VPN CloudHub for VPN connections
mentions TGW or two DXGWs as a way to enable DX-to-DX intentionally

overall.summary: with_skill wins overall (3 vs 0 criterion wins out of 3 judgments, avg confidence: medium).

criteria.reasoning: Both outputs correctly identify that a shared VGW or single DX Gateway cannot route traffic between two VIFs, and that a Transit Gateway with two DX Gateway attachments is the supported solution. Output B goes further in accuracy by correctly noting the mechanism (only VPC CIDRs are advertised to VIFs on a shared VGW/DXGW) and adds the nuance about Allowed Prefix Lists being required on the DXGW-TGW attachment for remote on-prem prefixes to propagate — this is a real and important technical detail for DX-to-DX via TGW designs that Output A omits. Output B also correctly distinguishes DX+VPN CloudHub behavior as a separate case. Output A's explanation is correct but less precise about why the TGW design works (it says 'the route tables permit it' without mentioning the critical Allowed Prefix List requirement, which is often what actually blocks or allows this routing in real DX+TGW setups). Output A's claim that this is 'the same underlying mechanism AWS documents for routing between two VPCs over two separate transit VIFs' is a reasonable analogy but somewhat vague.
criteria.evidence: Output B: 'The DXGW→TGW attachment can advertise more than just VPC CIDRs, so remote-site prefixes get propagated intentionally' and 'AWS advertises only the VPC CIDRs toward each VIF — not the other site's on-prem prefixes.' Output A: 'you can configure the TGW route tables so traffic flows from one DX attachment to the other' (less specific about prefix list requirement).

criteria.reasoning: Both outputs end with the same offer to validate the user's actual configuration, which is equally actionable. However, Output B provides a more structured, actionable breakdown with a clear table of scenarios that work vs. don't work, including the specific configuration detail (Allowed Prefix Lists) needed to make the TGW design function for remote-site routing, plus an alternative customer-side hairpin option. This gives the user more concrete decision points and alternative paths to consider before even validating their setup.
criteria.evidence: Output B's table lists concrete designs: 'Two DX Gateways into one Transit Gateway', 'TGW with an Allowed Prefix List', 'DX + VPN sharing a VGW', 'Customer-side hairpin' — each with a specific mechanism. Output A offers only one working design (transit VIF + TGW) without the prefix list caveat or alternative hairpin option.

criteria.reasoning: Output B covers more scenarios and edge cases: it explicitly addresses two DX VIFs on the same VGW, two DX VIFs on the same DXGW, the TGW-based solution with the prefix list nuance, the DX+VPN CloudHub case, and the customer-side hairpin alternative. Output A only covers two scenarios (VGW/private VIF hairpin restriction, and TGW via transit VIF), omitting the Allowed Prefix List nuance, the DX+VPN CloudHub distinction, and the customer-side hairpin alternative that Output B includes.
criteria.evidence: Output B's scenario table covers 4 distinct designs/configurations, while Output A covers only 2 (the 'No' case with VGW/DXGW hairpin restriction, and the 'Yes' case with transit VIF + TGW).

dx-prefer-one-location.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task about BGP/AS-path prepending recommendations. The triggering behavior fired as expected (1/1).

Expected output: Both variants met the expected output in their single trial (1/1, 100%). Confidence in that judgment was high for with_skill and only medium for without_skill, so without_skill's "met expectations" result rests on a somewhat weaker measurement.

Assertions (based on a single run each, so limited sample size): with_skill passed all 4/4 assertions, without_skill passed 3/4 (75%). Three of the four assertions passed for both variants ("recommends LP communities with higher preference on primary," "warns cross-region AS-path prepending is unreliable," and "does not contain 'error'") — these did not differentiate the variants. The one assertion that split the two was "explains AS-path prepending is reliable only within the same region," which with_skill passed with high confidence and without_skill failed (with only medium confidence in that failing grade). This is the single clearest difference between the variants in this eval, though it rests on one run and a non-high-confidence judgment for without_skill.

Quality comparison: Across the one pair evaluated, with_skill was favored on all three criteria (accuracy, actionability, completeness) with high confidence, and without_skill was not favored on any. This aligns directionally with the assertion gap above, but it's based on only one comparison pair, so it should be treated as a single data point rather than a robust trend.

Runtime and cost: with_skill took longer (~31s vs ~12s, about 19s more) and cost more (~$0.26 vs ~$0.10) than without_skill. Both stayed under the 30s runtime threshold check in the comparison data (0 runs exceeding threshold reported), and context window utilization was low and similar for both (5.1% vs 4.2%, no compaction for either). So with_skill's extra time/cost coincides with the higher quality and assertion-pass scores in this one task — a tradeoff rather than a clear deficiency either way.

Output consistency: Not measured (both variants show null for overall consistency), so there's no data here on run-to-run stability for either variant.

Overall, this is a single-task, single-run evaluation, which limits how much weight any of these findings should carry. Within that limited sample, with_skill showed higher assertion pass rate and was favored on all quality criteria, while taking longer and costing more; without_skill was faster and cheaper but missed one specific explanatory assertion (about AS-path prepending reliability being same-region-only) and had lower confidence in some of its graded outcomes. No consistency data exists to indicate whether these results would replicate across repeated runs.

Overall Output B's technical framework (path selection order, BFD, region-association caveats) appears more aligned with documented AWS behavior and is more internally consistent.

criteria.reasoning: Output B provides more concrete, verifiable action items: specific CLI commands (describe-connections, describe-virtual-interfaces, list-virtual-interface-routes) to verify VIF region association and current BGP advertisements before and after changes. It also recommends BFD configuration for fast failover and suggests testing in non-production before cutover with a blue/green rollout approach. Output B's guidance is more operationally actionable and includes concrete tools/commands the user can run immediately.

Output A covers the core BGP community/AS-path mechanism and warns about several common mistakes (same community on both sides, extended communities, forgetting both directions) but misses failover speed (BFD), topology considerations (TGW/Cloud WAN), verification tooling, and the region-association subtlety. Output A is more narrowly focused while Output B addresses a broader and more complete set of considerations relevant to a real-world DX failover design question.

criteria.reasoning: AWS's documented behavior for a VGW is that routes learned via Direct Connect are always preferred over VPN-learned routes for identical/equal-length prefixes, and this preference is a hard-coded path-type preference at the VGW, not something influenced by BGP attributes like AS-path or local preference on the AWS side. Output B correctly states this as a hard VGW behavior that cannot be overridden by local preference/AS-path/MED when prefixes match, and correctly notes that longest-prefix-match overrides the DX/VPN attachment-type preference when prefixes actually differ in length. Output A's claim that 'if prefix lengths are equal, AWS prefers DX' is directionally correct, but A incorrectly implies this preference could be influenced/confused by AS-path prepending ('if prefix lengths match, AWS uses DX regardless of AS_PATH length') -- which is actually correct, but then A also conflates mechanisms in a confusing way in the first paragraph about VPN advertising more specific prefixes due to the 20-prefix limit, when in fact the AWS max-prefix VPN/DX limits are different limits (100 prefixes typically) and conflates the allowed-prefix quota incorrectly. Output B's structure separating VPC->on-prem (AWS-controlled, DX always wins baseline) from on-prem->VPC (customer-controlled via local pref) is clearer and more aligned with how AWS documents this behavior (local pref on customer side influences inbound-to-AWS path for symmetric prefixes, but AWS side route selection for return traffic prefers DX).

Output B provides concrete validation commands (AWS CLI calls) to check VIF, connection, VPN, VGW, and route table states, plus a clear prioritized list of configuration strategies (active/passive design, matching local preference on customer router for symmetric behavior, deliberate longest-prefix-match approach for load-sharing, failover design, and stateless design considerations). It also explicitly states assumptions it made, inviting correction. Output A offers specific BGP local-preference values (200 vs 100) and a offer to pull actual BGP attributes, which is useful, but lacks concrete command examples and is less structured with actionable steps. Both end with an offer to continue, but B's structured steps and runnable commands give slightly more actionable specifics overall.

Output B covers the AWS-side path preference, the customer-side preference mechanism, the failure mode causing asymmetry, multiple strategies to avoid or intentionally control routing behavior (including a longest-prefix-match design option and failover-only design), plus operational considerations (ECMP behavior, stateless failover tolerance) and includes verification commands and stated assumptions. Output A covers the prefix-length and local-preference considerations but is narrower in scope, missing the nuance that DX preference is a hard attachment-type preference (not just tie-broken by equal prefix length) and lacks the operational commands, failure-mode narrative, and alternative design options B provides. B's broader treatment of both failure modes and design strategies makes it more complete.

Given this is based on one task with no consistency or quality-comparison data available, the efficiency differences should be weighed as a minor tradeoff alongside the correctness gap rather than treated as an independent strength, and the overall finding should be read with the caveat that it rests on a single test case.

cloudwan-overlapping-supernet.summary:
This single chat-task eval tested a scenario about longest-prefix-match routing shadowing on-prem hosts inside a VPC CIDR. The trigger condition for the test fired successfully (1/1).

On "expected output" — a holistic pass/fail judgment — with_skill met it (1/1, 100%) while without_skill did not (0/1, 0%). Both of these judgments were made with high confidence, so this is a meaningful, well-supported divergence between the two variants on the overall task outcome, even though it comes from a single test case.

This divergence is not reflected in the per-assertion breakdown, however: both with_skill and without_skill passed all four individual assertions (4/4, 100% each), covering explanation of the longest-prefix-match shadowing behavior, recommending non-overlapping address planning, mentioning Cloud WAN Routing Policies for prefix filtering on the Direct Connect attachment, and avoiding the word "error." All four assertions passed for both variants with high confidence, meaning none of them differentiate the variants — the gap seen in the expected-output judgment is not explained by any specific assertion failure, suggesting the expected-output criteria captured something beyond what the four assertions check for (e.g., overall coherence, correctness, or framing not covered by the discrete checks).

On cost and runtime, without_skill was somewhat faster (1m18s vs 1m30s, about 12s less) and cheaper ($0.65 vs $0.75), while context window utilization was nearly identical (5.3% vs 5.6%, no compaction for either). These are minor differences and, given only one task was run, not strongly conclusive on their own.

No direct quality comparison could be made: the quality comparison pair was skipped (0 evaluated, 1 skipped), so there's no additional signal on relative output quality beyond the expected-output judgment. Output consistency data is also absent (null) for both variants, so repeat-run stability could not be assessed.

Overall, this is a single-task eval with a notable split on the holistic expected-output judgment favoring with_skill, despite identical and perfect performance on the itemized assertions, and with without_skill showing marginally lower cost and runtime. Given the small sample size (one task), the missing quality-comparison data, and the lack of consistency data, this result should be treated as a limited, single-instance signal rather than a robust conclusion about either variant's overall quality.
